title: Subject-Verb Agreement (Syntax)
pyqFrequency: Appears in 3-5 questions in every Clerk/PO shift
overview: The fundamental principle that a singular subject takes a singular verb, and a plural subject takes a plural verb, with complex proximity and parenthetical rules.

rules.ruleTitle: Proximity Rule with Either/Or & Neither/Nor
rules.ruleHindiTitle: Either/Or और Neither/Nor में निकटता नियम
rules.formalRule: When two subjects are joined by 'either...or', 'neither...nor', 'not only...but also', or 'or', the verb agrees with the subject nearest to it.
rules.easyExplanation: Look at the subject closest to the verb! If the noun right before the verb is singular, make the verb singular; if it is plural, make the verb plural.
rules.correctExample: Neither the manager nor the cashiers were aware of the vault discrepancy.
rules.wrongExample: Neither the manager nor the cashiers was aware of the vault discrepancy.
rules.whyWrong: 'cashiers' is plural and sits closest to the verb, so the verb must be 'were', not 'was'.
rules.examShortcut: Cover everything before 'or' / 'nor' / 'but also' with your thumb! Read only the last subject + verb.
rules.commonTrap: Don't count both subjects together! It's not addition; only the nearest subject decides the verb.
rules.pyqReference: SBI Clerk Prelims 2024 Shift 2; IBPS Clerk 2023

rules.ruleTitle: Parenthetical Connectors (Along with, As well as, Together with)
rules.ruleHindiTitle: Along with, As well as के साथ प्रथम कर्ता नियम
rules.formalRule: When two subjects are connected by 'as well as', 'along with', 'together with', 'with', 'accompanied by', 'in addition to', 'like', 'unlike', 'except', the verb agrees with the FIRST subject.
rules.easyExplanation: Ignore the extra phrase between commas! The verb always listens ONLY to the very first main person or thing mentioned.
rules.correctExample: The Chief Executive Officer, along with senior branch managers, has approved the new retail lending policy.
rules.wrongExample: The Chief Executive Officer, along with senior branch managers, have approved the new retail lending policy.
rules.whyWrong: 'Chief Executive Officer' is singular and is the FIRST subject. 'along with senior branch managers' is just parenthetical information.
rules.examShortcut: Cross out the phrase starting from 'as well as / along with' until the comma or verb. The original subject stands bare.
rules.commonTrap: Examiners will place a huge plural noun list right before the verb to trick your ear into picking a plural verb.
rules.pyqReference: IBPS Clerk Mains 2023 Shift 1; SBI Clerk 2022

rules.ruleTitle: 'One of the' + Plural Noun + Relative Pronoun vs Simple Clause
rules.ruleHindiTitle: 'One of the' के बाद क्रिया का निर्धारण
rules.formalRule: 'One of + plural noun' takes a singular verb. BUT 'One of + plural noun + who/which/that' takes a PLURAL verb (agreeing with the plural antecedent). However, 'The ONLY one of + plural noun + who/which/that' takes a SINGULAR verb.
rules.easyExplanation: If 'who/that' refers to the group of people, use a plural verb. But if 'the ONLY one' is used, there is only one person, so use a singular verb!
rules.correctExample: He is one of those officers who have consistently exceeded their quarterly recovery targets.
rules.wrongExample: He is one of those officers who has consistently exceeded their quarterly recovery targets.
rules.whyWrong: 'who' refers back to 'those officers' (plural), so the relative clause requires 'have', not 'has'.
rules.examShortcut: Formula: 'One of the' + Plural Noun = Singular Verb. 'One of the' + Plural Noun + who/that = PLURAL Verb. 'The only one of the' + who/that = SINGULAR Verb.
rules.commonTrap: Missing the 'who/that' clause and defaulting to singular because of the word 'One'.
rules.pyqReference: IBPS RRB Officer Scale-I 2023; SBI Clerk Mains 2021

rules.ruleTitle: 'A number of' vs 'The number of'
rules.ruleHindiTitle: 'A number of' बनाम 'The number of'
rules.formalRule: 'A number of' denotes 'many' and takes a PLURAL verb. 'The number of' specifies a single mathematical figure/statistic and takes a SINGULAR verb.
rules.easyExplanation: 'A number of' = A lot of (Plural). 'The number of' = A specific count/digit (Singular).
rules.correctExample: The number of non-performing loans in the agricultural sector has steadily declined.
rules.wrongExample: The number of non-performing loans in the agricultural sector have steadily declined.
rules.whyWrong: We are referring to 'The number' (the metric/quantity), which is singular.
rules.examShortcut: A = Many (Plural verb). The = Definite figure (Singular verb).
rules.commonTrap: Seeing 'loans' right before 'has' and changing it to 'have'.

rules.ruleTitle: Units of Measurement, Distance, Time, and Money
rules.ruleHindiTitle: माप, दूरी, समय और मुद्रा की इकाइयाँ
rules.formalRule: When a plural noun denotes a specific quantity, amount, distance, or period considered as a single unit or whole, the verb is singular.
rules.easyExplanation: Think of the total sum or distance as one single lump or package. 10 kilometers is one distance. 50,000 rupees is one sum.
rules.correctExample: Fifty thousand rupees is a substantial amount for an unsecured micro-loan.
rules.wrongExample: Fifty thousand rupees are a substantial amount for an unsecured micro-loan.
rules.whyWrong: 'Fifty thousand rupees' is viewed here as a single unified amount of money.
rules.examShortcut: If the sentence uses 'a substantial amount / a long distance / a long time' in the predicate, the subject is acting as a single unit (Singular verb).
rules.commonTrap: If the money is spent individually on different items, it becomes plural: 'The rupees were distributed among the workers.'

title: Tenses & Aspect (Verb Timelines)
pyqFrequency: 2-3 questions per paper in Error Detection & Sentence Improvement
overview: Mastering precise time markers, past perfect double actions, stative verbs, and sequence of tenses across independent and subordinate clauses.

rules.ruleTitle: Simple Past with Specific Past Time Markers
rules.ruleHindiTitle: निश्चित भूतकाल समय सूचकों के साथ Simple Past
rules.formalRule: When a sentence contains a definite past time adverb (yesterday, ago, last night, last year, in 1947, on Monday), Simple Past (V2) MUST be used, NOT Present Perfect.
rules.easyExplanation: If you see a calendar date or past time word (like 'yesterday', 'ago', 'in 2021'), you cannot use 'have/has'!
rules.correctExample: The Reserve Bank of India lowered the benchmark repo rate by 25 basis points yesterday.
rules.wrongExample: The Reserve Bank of India has lowered the benchmark repo rate by 25 basis points yesterday.
rules.whyWrong: 'Yesterday' anchors the event in finished past time, which rejects the present connection of 'has lowered'.
rules.examShortcut: Look for words like: yesterday, ago, last month, in 2020. If present, strike out 'have/has' immediately!
rules.commonTrap: In spoken Indian English, people often say 'I have seen him yesterday', which banking exams aggressively penalize.
rules.pyqReference: SBI Clerk Mains 2024 Shift 1; IBPS Clerk Prelims 2023

rules.ruleTitle: Double Past Actions (Past Perfect + Simple Past)
rules.ruleHindiTitle: दोहरे भूतकाल कार्य (Past Perfect + Simple Past)
rules.formalRule: When two actions happened in the past, the earlier completed action takes Past Perfect (had + V3), and the subsequent action takes Simple Past (V2).
rules.easyExplanation: The first action that finished gets 'had + 3rd form'. The second action that followed gets normal past tense (V2).
rules.correctExample: The fraudulent transactions had already cleared before the cybersecurity team isolated the compromised server.
rules.wrongExample: The fraudulent transactions already cleared before the cybersecurity team isolated the compromised server.
rules.whyWrong: Clearing the transactions occurred BEFORE the isolation, so it requires 'had already cleared'.
rules.examShortcut: First past action = had + V3. Second past action = V2.
rules.commonTrap: Using 'had' with both actions: 'The train had left before he had reached the station' is incorrect.
rules.pyqReference: IBPS Clerk Mains 2022; RRB Office Assistant 2021

rules.ruleTitle: Stative Verbs Prohibited in Continuous Tenses
rules.ruleHindiTitle: Stative Verbs का Continuous Tense में निषेध
rules.formalRule: Verbs of perception, cognition, emotion, and possession (know, understand, remember, believe, hear, smell, possess, own, consist) are stative and cannot be used in continuous (-ing) forms.
rules.easyExplanation: You cannot 'be knowing' something or 'be understanding' a concept in standard English. Use Simple Present: 'I know', 'I understand'.
rules.correctExample: The branch auditor now understands the mechanism behind the reconciliation failure.
rules.wrongExample: The branch auditor is now understanding the mechanism behind the reconciliation failure.
rules.whyWrong: 'Understand' is a mental state, not a physical action in progress; it rejects the continuous tense.
rules.examShortcut: Check -ing words following 'is/are/was/were'. If it is a feeling, sense, or thought verb, it is almost certainly the error!
rules.commonTrap: Confusing action uses with stative uses: 'The soup tastes delicious' (stative) vs 'The chef is tasting the soup' (active physical action).

rules.ruleTitle: Since vs For with Perfect & Perfect Continuous Tenses
rules.ruleHindiTitle: Since और For का सटीक प्रयोग
rules.formalRule: 'Since' denotes a specific point in time (since 2018, since Monday, since morning). 'For' denotes a duration or period of time (for 5 years, for two hours). Both must be used with Perfect or Perfect Continuous tenses.
rules.easyExplanation: 'Since' = Starting point / clock or calendar date. 'For' = Total counted time (number of days, years, hours).
rules.correctExample: She has been working in the treasury department for the last six years.
rules.wrongExample: She is working in the treasury department since the last six years.
rules.whyWrong: Two errors: Using Present Continuous ('is working') instead of Present Perfect Continuous, and using 'since' for a period of time.
rules.examShortcut: Period of time (counted numbers like 2 days, 5 years) = FOR. Exact naming of starting moment = SINCE.
rules.commonTrap: 'For the past...' takes 'for', not 'since'.

title: Conditional Sentences (Hypothetical & Real)
pyqFrequency: Frequently tested in Sentence Improvement and Error Detection
overview: Mastering the structural pairing of condition clauses (if-clauses) and result clauses across Types 0, 1, 2, 3, and inverted structures.

rules.ruleTitle: Third Conditional (Unfulfilled Past Condition)
rules.ruleHindiTitle: तीसरी शर्त: भूतकाल की अपूर्ण स्थिति
rules.formalRule: If + Past Perfect (had + V3) ➔ Result clause: would have / could have / might have + V3. Alternatively, inverted structure: Had + Subject + V3 ➔ would have + V3.
rules.easyExplanation: If 'had + 3rd form' appears in the 'if' part, the result MUST have 'would have + 3rd form'. Never put 'would have' inside the 'if' clause!
rules.correctExample: If the compliance officer had scrutinized the KYC documents, the bank would have prevented the money laundering attempt.
rules.wrongExample: If the compliance officer would have scrutinized the KYC documents, the bank would have prevented the money laundering attempt.
rules.whyWrong: 'Would have' cannot appear in the conditional ('if') clause. The condition must take 'had + V3'.
rules.examShortcut: If-clause CANNOT take 'would', 'could', or 'will'. Scan the 'if' part immediately for forbidden modals!
rules.commonTrap: Inversion trap: 'Had the compliance officer scrutinized...' means 'If the officer had scrutinized...'. Both are identical and correct.

rules.ruleTitle: Second Conditional (Improbable/Unreal Present Condition)
rules.ruleHindiTitle: दूसरी शर्त: काल्पनिक या अवास्तविक वर्तमान
rules.formalRule: If + Simple Past (Subjunctive 'were' for all persons) ➔ Result clause: would + V1.
rules.easyExplanation: In an imaginary or hypothetical scenario, use 'WERE' with all subjects (I, he, she, it). Then use 'would + base verb'.
rules.correctExample: If he were the Governor of the Reserve Bank, he would implement stricter liquidity requirements.
rules.wrongExample: If he was the Governor of the Reserve Bank, he would implement stricter liquidity requirements.
rules.whyWrong: In hypothetical subjunctive conditions, 'were' is grammatically mandatory even for singular pronouns like 'he' or 'I'.
rules.examShortcut: Look for 'If I was you' or 'If he was the manager' ➔ instantly replace 'was' with 'were'.
rules.commonTrap: Thinking 'he was' is correct because 'he' is singular. In subjunctive conditionals, 'was' is an error.
rules.pyqReference: IBPS RRB Clerk Mains 2023; SBI Clerk 2020

rules.ruleTitle: First Conditional (Probable Future Condition)
rules.ruleHindiTitle: पहली शर्त: संभावित भविष्य
rules.formalRule: If + Simple Present (V1/V5) ➔ Result clause: will / can / may + V1. Never use 'will' in both clauses.
rules.easyExplanation: When talking about future conditions, keep the 'if' clause in simple present. Only the result clause gets 'will'.
rules.correctExample: If inflation remains elevated in the upcoming quarter, the monetary policy committee will hike interest rates.
rules.wrongExample: If inflation will remain elevated in the upcoming quarter, the monetary policy committee will hike interest rates.
rules.whyWrong: Two 'will's in one conditional sentence is grammatically invalid. The conditional clause must be in Simple Present.
rules.examShortcut: Formula: If + Present ➔ Will + V1. No double 'will' allowed!
rules.commonTrap: Same rule applies to time conjunctions: 'when', 'as soon as', 'until', 'unless' also take Simple Present, not 'will'.

title: Articles & Determiners
pyqFrequency: 1-2 questions per shift, often combined with noun modifiers
overview: Indefinite articles based on phonetics (sound, not letter), definite article usage with unique geographical and political entities, and zero-article rules.

rules.ruleTitle: Sound-Based Indefinite Articles (Phonetics Rule)
rules.ruleHindiTitle: ध्वनि आधारित उपपद नियम (Phonetics)
rules.formalRule: 'A' is used before words beginning with a consonant sound. 'An' is used before words beginning with a vowel sound (a, e, i, o, u phonemes).
rules.easyExplanation: Listen to the pronunciation, do not look at the spelling! A vowel sound gets 'an'; a consonant sound gets 'a'.
rules.correctExample: He submitted an FIR regarding the ATM skimming fraud to a European investigator.
rules.wrongExample: He submitted a FIR regarding the ATM skimming fraud to an European investigator.
rules.whyWrong: 'FIR' is pronounced 'Ef-Eye-Ahr' (starts with vowel sound 'e' ➔ 'an FIR'). 'European' is pronounced 'Yoo-ro-pe-an' (starts with consonant sound 'y' ➔ 'a European').
rules.examShortcut: Acronym test: If the first letter sound starts with a vowel (F = ef, H = aitch, M = em, N = en, S = es, X = ex), use 'AN'.
rules.commonTrap: 'An honest' (h is silent), 'A university' (starts with 'yu' consonant sound), 'An heirloom', 'A one-rupee coin' (starts with 'w' sound).
rules.pyqReference: SBI Clerk Prelims 2023; RRB Office Assistant 2022

rules.ruleTitle: The Definite Article with Comparative Structures
rules.ruleHindiTitle: तुलनात्मक संरचना में 'The' का प्रयोग
rules.formalRule: When parallel progression or comparison is expressed using 'The more... the more...', both comparative adjectives require the definite article 'the'.
rules.easyExplanation: When two things increase or decrease together, put 'THE' in front of both sides: 'The higher you climb, the colder it gets.'
rules.correctExample: The greater the credit risk of the borrower, the higher the lending interest rate.
rules.wrongExample: Greater the credit risk of the borrower, higher the lending interest rate.
rules.whyWrong: Both comparative phrases in a parallel proportional structure must be preceded by 'the'.
rules.examShortcut: Pattern check: 'The + comparative... the + comparative'. If either 'the' is missing, that is your error!
rules.commonTrap: Omitting 'the' before the second comparative clause.

rules.ruleTitle: Zero Article with Abstract Nouns, Meals, and Sports
rules.ruleHindiTitle: Zero Article (उपपद का अभाव)
rules.formalRule: No article is used before abstract nouns, materials, names of meals (breakfast, lunch, dinner), languages, and sports when used in a general sense.
rules.easyExplanation: Do not put 'the' in front of general words like 'honesty', 'gold', 'dinner', or 'cricket' unless you are talking about a specific instance.
rules.correctExample: Integrity is the most critical attribute required in commercial banking.
rules.wrongExample: The integrity is the most critical attribute required in the commercial banking.
rules.whyWrong: 'Integrity' is an abstract noun used in a general sense, so it cannot take the definite article 'the'.
rules.examShortcut: Is it a specific item or general quality? If general, drop 'the'.
rules.commonTrap: If followed by 'of', it becomes specific and takes 'the': 'The integrity of the internal auditor was questioned.' (Correct).

title: Prepositions & Fixed Prepositional Collocations
pyqFrequency: 3-4 questions per shift in Error Detection, Fillers, and Phrase Replacement
overview: Mastering fixed prepositions, subtle distinctions between pairs (between/among, beside/besides, into/in), and verbs that take no prepositions.

rules.ruleTitle: Fixed Prepositions with High-Yield Banking Verbs
rules.ruleHindiTitle: बैंकिंग क्रियाओं के साथ निश्चित पूर्वसर्ग
rules.formalRule: Certain verbs and adjectives are strictly accompanied by specific prepositions: 'abide by', 'abstain from', 'adhere to', 'accused of', 'conducive to', 'prohibit from', 'prevent from', 'deprive of', 'cope with'.
rules.easyExplanation: In English, certain words are married to specific prepositions. You cannot change their partners!
rules.correctExample: All scheduled commercial banks must adhere to the prompt corrective action guidelines.
rules.wrongExample: All scheduled commercial banks must adhere with the prompt corrective action guidelines.
rules.whyWrong: 'Adhere' takes the fixed preposition 'to', never 'with'.
rules.examShortcut: Exam Favorites: 'cope with' (NOT 'cope up with'), 'comply with' (NOT 'comply to'), 'refrain from', 'adhere to'.
rules.commonTrap: 'Cope up with' is universally used in spoken Indian English but is 100% incorrect in banking exams; the correct idiom is 'cope with'.
rules.pyqReference: SBI Clerk Mains 2024 Shift 2; IBPS Clerk 2023

rules.ruleTitle: Verbs that Reject Prepositions (Direct Transitive Verbs)
rules.ruleHindiTitle: पूर्वसर्ग रहित सकर्मक क्रियाएँ
rules.formalRule: Transitive verbs such as 'discuss', 'describe', 'order', 'request', 'reach', 'resemble', 'enter', 'attack', 'accompany', and 'comprise' take their objects directly without prepositions in active voice.
rules.easyExplanation: Do not put words like 'about', 'to', or 'into' after words like 'discuss', 'order', or 'enter' (a place)!
rules.correctExample: The asset liability committee met to discuss the non-performing loan portfolio.
rules.wrongExample: The asset liability committee met to discuss about the non-performing loan portfolio.
rules.whyWrong: 'Discuss' means 'to talk about'. Adding 'about' creates a redundant preposition error.
rules.examShortcut: Disallowed pairs: 'discuss about', 'order for', 'resemble with', 'enter into (a room)', 'comprise of'.
rules.commonTrap: 'Comprise' does NOT take 'of' in active voice ('The board comprises five directors'). However, in passive voice, 'is comprised of' is acceptable.

rules.ruleTitle: Between vs Among
rules.ruleHindiTitle: Between बनाम Among
rules.formalRule: 'Between' is used for two distinct entities, or for more than two when expressing mutual bilateral relationships/treaties. 'Among' is used for more than two entities viewed as an undivided group.
rules.easyExplanation: 'Between' is usually for 2 things. 'Among' is for 3 or more members of a crowd or group.
rules.correctExample: There is a formal bilateral currency swap agreement between the two central banks.
rules.wrongExample: There is a formal bilateral currency swap agreement among the two central banks.
rules.whyWrong: There are only two central banks involved, so 'between' is mandatory.
rules.examShortcut: 2 items = Between. 3+ items in a collective group = Among. Treaty/relation between multiple named countries = Between.
rules.commonTrap: 'Between each...' or 'between every...' is incorrect. Say 'between this and that'.

title: Conjunctions & Correlative Pairs
pyqFrequency: 2-3 questions per shift in Error Detection, Fillers, and Connectors
overview: Rigorous pairing of correlative conjunctions, parallel structures following correlative pairs, and inverted negative conjunctions.

rules.ruleTitle: Strict Correlative Conjunction Pairings
rules.ruleHindiTitle: सहसम्बन्धी संयोजकों के निश्चित जोड़े
rules.formalRule: Correlative conjunctions must strictly pair: 'Scarcely / Hardly... when', 'No sooner... than', 'Barely... when', 'Not only... but also', 'Neither... nor', 'Either... or', 'Lest... should', 'Although / Though... yet (or comma)'.
rules.easyExplanation: Learn these exact pairs like phone numbers! You can never mix 'No sooner' with 'when', or 'Hardly' with 'than'.
rules.correctExample: No sooner had the branch opened than a swarm of customers arrived for sovereign gold bonds.
rules.wrongExample: No sooner had the branch opened when a swarm of customers arrived for sovereign gold bonds.
rules.whyWrong: 'No sooner' must strictly be paired with 'than', never with 'when' or 'then'.
rules.examShortcut: Pair Checklist: No sooner ➔ than. Hardly/Scarcely ➔ when. Lest ➔ should. Although ➔ yet.
rules.commonTrap: Examiners will frequently substitute 'then' for 'than' with 'No sooner' (spelling trap).
rules.pyqReference: SBI Clerk Mains 2023 Shift 2; IBPS Clerk 2022

rules.ruleTitle: Parallelism with 'Not only... but also'
rules.ruleHindiTitle: 'Not only... but also' के साथ समानांतर संरचना
rules.formalRule: The parts of speech following 'not only' and 'but also' must be strictly parallel (noun with noun, verb with verb, prepositional phrase with prepositional phrase).
rules.easyExplanation: Whatever grammatical unit sits right after 'but also' MUST match what sits right after 'not only'!
rules.correctExample: The bank not only restructured the debt but also reduced the penal interest rate.
rules.wrongExample: The bank not only restructured the debt but also the penal interest rate was reduced.
rules.whyWrong: 'Not only' is followed by a verb phrase ('restructured the debt'), but 'but also' is followed by a clause ('the penal interest rate was reduced'). They must be parallel.
rules.examShortcut: Look at what comes immediately after 'but also'. Then reposition 'not only' so it sits before the exact same grammatical element.
rules.commonTrap: Placing 'not only' before the subject instead of before the verb.

rules.ruleTitle: Lest + Should (Avoidance of Double Negatives)
rules.ruleHindiTitle: Lest + Should और दोहरे नकारात्मक का निषेध
rules.formalRule: 'Lest' means 'for fear that' or 'so that not'. It must be followed by 'should' (or subjunctive base verb). Because 'lest' is inherently negative, 'not' CANNOT be used with it.
rules.easyExplanation: 'Lest' already means 'kahin aisa na ho jaye'. Therefore, never write 'not' with 'lest', and always pair it with 'should'!
rules.correctExample: Verify the customer's signature carefully lest the clearing house should reject the instrument.
rules.wrongExample: Verify the customer's signature carefully lest the clearing house should not reject the instrument.
rules.whyWrong: 'Lest' already contains negative meaning; adding 'not' creates an illicit double negative.
rules.examShortcut: Lest + Subject + SHOULD (No 'not', no 'will', no 'may').
rules.commonTrap: Using 'may' or 'will' instead of 'should': 'Lest you will fail' is incorrect.

title: Adjectives, Adverbs & Inversion
pyqFrequency: 2-3 questions per shift in Error Detection & Sentence Improvement
overview: Latin comparative adjectives (senior to), order of adjectives, adverbial inversion with negative qualifiers, and confusing modifier pairs.

rules.ruleTitle: Latin Comparatives Ending in -or (Preposition 'To' vs 'Than')
rules.ruleHindiTitle: -or पर समाप्त होने वाले लैटिन तुलनात्मक विशेषण
rules.formalRule: Adjectives of Latin origin ending in '-or' (senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior, anterior, posterior) as well as 'preferable' take the preposition 'to', NEVER 'than'.
rules.easyExplanation: Words ending in '-or' (senior, junior, prior) plus 'preferable' hate the word 'than'. Always use 'TO'!
rules.correctExample: Her operational banking experience is superior to that of any other applicant.
rules.wrongExample: Her operational banking experience is superior than that of any other applicant.
rules.whyWrong: 'Superior' takes the preposition 'to', never 'than'.
rules.examShortcut: If an adjective ends in '-or' or is 'preferable', scan immediately for 'than' and replace it with 'to'. Also never use 'more' before them ('more superior' is redundant).
rules.commonTrap: 'More preferable than' is a triple error: drop 'more' and change 'than' to 'to' ➔ 'preferable to'.

rules.ruleTitle: Negative Adverb Inversion (Hardly, Scarcely, Seldom, Little)
rules.ruleHindiTitle: नकारात्मक क्रियाविशेषण के साथ Inversion नियम
rules.formalRule: When a sentence begins with a negative or restrictive adverb (hardly, scarcely, seldom, rarely, barely, neither, nor, under no circumstances, little), inverted word order (Auxiliary Verb + Subject + Main Verb) must be used.
rules.easyExplanation: When you put words like 'Seldom', 'Hardly', or 'Never' at the very beginning of a sentence, the helping verb jumps in front of the subject!
rules.correctExample: Seldom has the Monetary Policy Committee witnessed such consensus among its external members.
rules.wrongExample: Seldom the Monetary Policy Committee has witnessed such consensus among its external members.
rules.whyWrong: Starting with 'Seldom' mandates inversion: auxiliary 'has' must precede the subject.
rules.examShortcut: Formula: Negative Adverb + Helping Verb + Subject + Main Verb.
rules.commonTrap: In past tense: 'Hardly he saw' ➔ Correct: 'Hardly did he see' or 'Hardly had he seen'.

rules.ruleTitle: Little vs A Little vs The Little (and Few vs A Few)
rules.ruleHindiTitle: Little / A Little / The Little का सूक्ष्म अंतर
rules.formalRule: 'Little' (uncountable) / 'Few' (countable) = Almost none (negative meaning). 'A little' / 'A few' = Some, a small quantity (positive meaning). 'The little' / 'The few' = The specific small amount that remains.
rules.easyExplanation: Without 'a' = Negative (practically nothing). With 'a' = Positive (at least some). With 'the' = Whatever specific amount was there.
rules.correctExample: There was little hope of loan recovery because the borrower had declared bankruptcy.
rules.wrongExample: There was a little hope of loan recovery because the borrower had declared bankruptcy.
rules.whyWrong: Bankruptcy implies there is virtually NO hope (negative context), so the negative word 'little' is required, not 'a little'.
rules.examShortcut: Context clue: Does the sentence describe failure, sadness, or lack? Use 'little/few'. Does it describe some progress? Use 'a little/a few'.
rules.commonTrap: Using 'few' with uncountable nouns (money, time, advice) instead of 'little'.

title: Nouns, Pronouns & Case Concord
pyqFrequency: 2-3 questions per shift in Error Detection
overview: Uncountable nouns masquerading as plurals, singular-plural pairs, order of personal pronouns (231 rule), and relative pronoun usage (who vs whom).

rules.ruleTitle: Inherently Uncountable Nouns with No Plural Forms
rules.ruleHindiTitle: नित्य एकवचन अगणनीय संज्ञाएँ
rules.formalRule: Nouns such as 'furniture', 'information', 'scenery', 'luggage', 'baggage', 'advice', 'equipment', 'machinery', 'poetry', 'bread', 'alphabet' are strictly uncountable. They cannot take 's/es' or indefinite articles 'a/an'.
rules.easyExplanation: Words like 'information', 'furniture', and 'luggage' can never end with 's' and can never have 'an information' in front of them!
rules.correctExample: The auditor requested detailed pieces of information regarding the offshore accounts.
rules.wrongExample: The auditor requested detailed informations regarding the offshore accounts.
rules.whyWrong: 'Information' is an uncountable noun and cannot be pluralized with '-s'.
rules.examShortcut: Look for words ending in '-s' like: furnitures, informations, sceneries, machineries. Instant error!
rules.commonTrap: To make them countable, say 'pieces of furniture', 'items of luggage', 'a word of advice'.

rules.ruleTitle: Order of Personal Pronouns (231 Rule vs 123 Rule)
rules.ruleHindiTitle: व्यक्तिवाचक सर्वनामों का क्रम (231 नियम बनाम 123 नियम)
rules.formalRule: In normal, polite, or pleasant contexts, pronouns must follow the 231 order (Second person ➔ Third person ➔ First person: You, he, and I). When confessing guilt, error, or in unpleasant contexts, use the 123 order (First ➔ Second ➔ Third: I, you, and he).
rules.easyExplanation: In good things: Put others first (You, he, and I = 231). In mistakes or faults: Take the blame first (I, you, and he = 123)!
rules.correctExample: You, he, and I have been selected to attend the national digital banking seminar.
rules.wrongExample: I, you, and he have been selected to attend the national digital banking seminar.
rules.whyWrong: In a positive accomplishment, etiquette dictates 2nd person (You) ➔ 3rd person (he) ➔ 1st person (I).
rules.examShortcut: Check pronoun sequence: Good news = 2 ➔ 3 ➔ 1. Blame/Apology = 1 ➔ 2 ➔ 3.
rules.commonTrap: 'He and you' or 'I and you' in polite business contexts.

rules.ruleTitle: Who vs Whom (Subjective vs Objective Case)
rules.ruleHindiTitle: Who बनाम Whom (कर्ता बनाम कर्म कारक)
rules.formalRule: 'Who' is a subjective pronoun (acts as the subject performing the verb). 'Whom' is an objective pronoun (acts as the recipient of the action or object of a preposition).
rules.easyExplanation: Substitute with 'He' or 'Him'! If 'he' fits, use 'WHO'. If 'him' fits, use 'WHOM'. (He = Who, Him = Whom).
rules.correctExample: The customer whom the branch manager interviewed yesterday has filed a formal grievance.
rules.wrongExample: The customer who the branch manager interviewed yesterday has filed a formal grievance.
rules.whyWrong: The branch manager interviewed HIM (object), so the relative pronoun must be 'whom'.
rules.examShortcut: Count the subjects and verbs! If Number of Verbs > Number of Subjects, you need 'WHO' to serve as a subject. If Verbs == Subjects, use 'WHOM'.
rules.commonTrap: Inserting parenthetical phrases like 'who they think...' to confuse the pronoun count.
rules.pyqReference: SBI Clerk Mains 2023; IBPS RRB Scale-I 2022

title: Non-Finite Verbs (Gerunds, Infinitives & Participles)
pyqFrequency: 2-3 questions per shift in Error Detection & Phrase Replacement
overview: Phrases with 'to' followed by gerunds, bare infinitives following causative and sensory verbs, and dangling participial modifiers.

rules.ruleTitle: Phrases with 'To' followed by Gerund (V1 + ing)
rules.ruleHindiTitle: 'To' के साथ Gerund (V1 + ing) वाले विशिष्ट मुहावरे
rules.formalRule: Although 'to' is normally followed by a bare infinitive (V1), prepositional phrases where 'to' is a true preposition must be followed by a GERUND (V1 + ing): 'look forward to', 'with a view to', 'accustomed to', 'given to', 'prone to', 'addicted to', 'devoted to', 'in addition to'.
rules.easyExplanation: Usually 'to' takes 1st form of verb (to go, to eat). BUT in phrases like 'look forward to' or 'with a view to', the 'to' is a preposition, so you MUST add '-ing'!
rules.correctExample: The treasury desk is looking forward to stabilizing foreign exchange reserves this quarter.
rules.wrongExample: The treasury desk is looking forward to stabilize foreign exchange reserves this quarter.
rules.whyWrong: 'Look forward to' is a fixed idiom taking a gerund, so it requires 'stabilizing', not 'stabilize'.
rules.examShortcut: High-frequency exam triggers: 'looking forward to + V-ing', 'with a view to + V-ing', 'used to + V-ing (when preceded by be/is/are/was)'.
rules.commonTrap: Defaulting to base verb V1 because of the presence of 'to'.
rules.pyqReference: SBI Clerk Mains 2024 Shift 1; IBPS Clerk 2023

rules.ruleTitle: Bare Infinitive without 'To' (Causative Verbs)
rules.ruleHindiTitle: Bare Infinitive ('To' रहित क्रिया)
rules.formalRule: Verbs of perception and causation like 'make', 'let', 'bid', 'watch', 'see', 'hear' take a bare infinitive (V1 without 'to') in the active voice.
rules.easyExplanation: After 'make', 'let', and 'see', do NOT use 'to'! Say 'He made me cry', NOT 'He made me to cry'.
rules.correctExample: The branch manager made the loan applicant submit certified tax returns.
rules.wrongExample: The branch manager made the loan applicant to submit certified tax returns.
rules.whyWrong: 'Made' is a causative verb and takes a bare infinitive ('submit'), not a full infinitive ('to submit').
rules.examShortcut: Causative pattern: Subject + make/let + Object + V1 (no 'to').
rules.commonTrap: In passive voice, 'make' DOES take 'to': 'He was made to submit the returns' is correct.
rules.pyqReference: IBPS Clerk Prelims 2022; RRB Office Assistant 2021

rules.ruleTitle: Dangling Participles (Unattached Modifiers)
rules.ruleHindiTitle: Dangling Participle (असंलग्न कृदंत)
rules.formalRule: A participial phrase at the start of a sentence must logically modify the grammatical subject immediately following the comma.
rules.easyExplanation: Whoever is doing the action in the opening phrase must be the subject right after the comma!
rules.correctExample: Walking through the currency chest, the inspector discovered an open security seal.
rules.wrongExample: Walking through the currency chest, an open security seal was discovered by the inspector.
rules.whyWrong: As written, 'an open security seal' appears to be the one 'walking through the currency chest'!
rules.examShortcut: Ask: WHO is doing the opening action? If it's not the subject right after the comma, it's a dangling modifier error.
rules.commonTrap: 'Being a rainy day, I could not go out' ➔ Incorrect! Correct: 'It being a rainy day, I could not go out.'

title: Parallelism & Superfluous Expressions
pyqFrequency: 1-2 questions per shift in Sentence Improvement & Error Detection
overview: Eliminating redundant words commonly used in colloquial speech and enforcing symmetrical grammatical structures in lists and comparisons.

rules.ruleTitle: Redundant/Superfluous Word Combinations
rules.ruleHindiTitle: निरर्थक और दोहराव वाले शब्द संयोजन
rules.formalRule: Combining words with overlapping meanings creates a grammatical redundancy: 'return back', 'repeat again', 'revert back', 'cousin brother', 'suppose if', 'blunder mistake', 'flee away', 'kindly requested'.
rules.easyExplanation: 'Re-' already means 'back' or 'again'. 'Return' already means go back. Saying 'return back' is saying 'back back'!
rules.correctExample: The customer service representative promised to revert to the account holder by Monday.
rules.wrongExample: The customer service representative promised to revert back to the account holder by Monday.
rules.whyWrong: 'Revert' already denotes going back to an earlier topic; 'back' is totally superfluous.
rules.examShortcut: Banned duplicates: 'revert back', 'return back', 'repeat again', 'suppose if', 'blend together', 'adequate enough'.
rules.commonTrap: 'Cousin brother/sister' is extremely common in colloquial Indian English, but banking exams consider it a strict grammatical error; use only 'cousin'.

rules.ruleTitle: Parallelism in Series and Lists
rules.ruleHindiTitle: सूचियों और श्रृंखलाओं में समानांतरता
rules.formalRule: All items joined by coordinating conjunctions (and, but, or) in a series must maintain identical grammatical forms (e.g., all gerunds, all infinitives, all noun phrases).
rules.easyExplanation: Keep the rhythm! If your first item is an '-ing' verb, all items must be '-ing' verbs: 'investing, trading, and saving'.
rules.correctExample: The digital strategy focuses on enhancing mobile UI, streamlining onboarding, and mitigating cyber risks.
rules.wrongExample: The digital strategy focuses on enhancing mobile UI, to streamline onboarding, and mitigating cyber risks.
rules.whyWrong: 'to streamline' breaks the parallel series of gerunds ('enhancing', 'mitigating').
rules.examShortcut: Inspect the series: Item 1 = Item 2 = Item 3. If one item shifts form, that item is your answer!
rules.commonTrap: Mixing clauses with phrases in a list of requirements.
